articles.headline: Singapore Aims to Be Regional Clinical Research Hub
articles.dek: The country is streamlining regulatory processes and fostering international partnerships to accelerate healthcare innovations and drug development.
articles.lead: Singapore is taking steps to become a leading regional center for clinical research and evidence generation. Health Minister Ong Ye Kung announced on Monday that the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) will implement measures to expedite regulatory processes for drug development and clinical trials.
articles.takeaway: The country is streamlining regulatory processes and fostering international partnerships to accelerate healthcare innovations and drug development.
body: Singapore is taking steps to become a leading regional center for clinical research and evidence generation. Health Minister Ong Ye Kung announced on Monday that the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) will implement measures to expedite regulatory processes for drug development and clinical trials.

Key initiatives include a new priority track, set to launch in November 2026, allowing selected health products to undergo simultaneous regulatory evaluation and health technology assessment. This aims to reduce assessment times significantly. Additionally, Singapore is establishing a "regulatory innovation corridor" with the United Kingdom to explore breakthrough therapies, including those utilizing artificial intelligence in drug development.

These efforts are expected to halve approval times for certain lower-risk Phase 3 clinical trials, reducing them from 30 days to 15 days. The time for the first health technology assessment decision could also be shortened from approximately one year to between six and nine months post-regulatory approval.

Minister Ong highlighted the need to simplify the journey for companies moving through research, clinical development, regulatory evaluation, and patient access, noting that current multi-agency hand-offs can cause delays and uncertainty. The HSA's regulatory approach is expanding across geographical boundaries, the healthcare value chain, and regulatory domains to create a more integrated system.

Singapore also seeks to leverage its regulatory approvals as a trusted gateway to larger regional markets, as many countries currently refer to HSA approvals to expedite their own processes. As part of the Access Consortium, Singapore aligns regulatory practices with other medium-sized regulatory authorities, sharing evaluation work and expertise. The nation is also pursuing World Health Organization listed authority status for vaccines, which could potentially speed up vaccine access while maintaining high safety standards.

He is accused of committing the offences between December 2024 and October 2025. Ong’s case will be mentioned again on Nov 6. body: The Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) is launching several new initiatives to bolster religious guidance, spiritual care, and community support services offered at mosques. These efforts are designed to better address the changing needs of the Muslim community.

Key components of the plan include the appointment of Mufti Associates across four mosque districts to provide localized religious guidance and mentorship. MUIS is also developing a structured Islamic Spiritual Care and Guidance framework to ensure a consistent approach to spiritual support, with training for religious personnel to identify and address spiritual care needs.

Furthermore, MUIS is expanding community outreach through its Qaryah networks, aiming to connect with residents who may be less engaged with mosque programs. Initiatives like Qaryah 2.0 and QaryahKITA are already reaching families in housing estates and the broader community, with a pilot program for seniors planned.

These announcements were made at the One Mosque Sector Townhall, where Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs Zaqy Mohamad emphasized the importance of safeguarding the trust placed in mosques and religious teachers. He highlighted the need for robust safeguards that do not compromise the welcoming nature of mosques, stating they must be both safe and open.

The initiatives follow a case of sexual abuse by a self-styled religious mentor, prompting MUIS to strengthen security measures. A Committee to Strengthen Safeguards in Religious Settings has also been formed to assess existing measures and recommend improvements for safer religious environments.

articles.dek: Minister Grace Fu states Singapore is ready to help Indonesia combat forest fires and mitigate the resulting haze, as air quality in Singapore remains in the unhealthy range.
articles.lead: Singapore's Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, Grace Fu, announced on Saturday, October 10, 2026, that the nation is prepared to assist Indonesia in combating forest fires. The ongoing haze has led to unhealthy air quality levels across Singapore.

body: Singapore's Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, Grace Fu, announced on Saturday, October 10, 2026, that the nation is prepared to assist Indonesia in combating forest fires. The ongoing haze has led to unhealthy air quality levels across Singapore.

Minister Fu has been in communication with her Indonesian counterpart, Minister Jumhur Hidayat, expressing support and acknowledging Indonesia's efforts to contain the fires. "We stand ready to assist where we can," Fu stated, emphasizing Singapore's concern for its citizens' well-being and its readiness to implement protective measures.

Air quality in Singapore saw some improvement overnight but remained in the unhealthy range on Saturday. The Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) readings varied across the island, with central Singapore recording 174 at 9 a.m. This follows a day where the central region reached a high of 192, the season's peak.

Contingency plans are in place for various air quality levels, including measures for the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix. The Haze Task Force has issued advisories for health, schools, workplaces, transport, and sporting activities. Schools may close if the air quality forecast enters the hazardous range, and healthcare institutions have activated preparedness measures.

Indonesia is experiencing its most severe forest and land fires in 11 years, exacerbated by super El Nino conditions. Official figures indicate significant land area burned, with satellite estimates showing a substantial increase by the end of August. Indonesia has established a new national agency for peatland and mangrove management and has suspended companies found with burned land within their concessions.

International partners, including Japan and Malaysia, have also offered assistance to Indonesia in firefighting operations. Singapore's offer of support is part of a broader regional effort to address the persistent haze issue.

body: Standard Chartered Group CEO Bill Winters has called for stronger regulation and increased international cooperation to manage the risks associated with artificial intelligence. Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore, Winters stated that AI requires more oversight than many other industries, noting the lengthy approval process for new drug formulations compared to the current lack of guardrails for AI.

Winters acknowledged that technology companies aim to develop AI responsibly but highlighted geopolitical competition, particularly between the US and China, as a factor necessitating global cooperation. He described the current situation as an "arms race" where AI is used for both developing new customer experiences and for defense against cyber threats.

While Standard Chartered is already utilizing AI to enhance efficiency and customer interactions, Winters warned that cybercriminals could also leverage the technology. He anticipates that negative incidents related to AI are likely to occur, despite ongoing efforts to develop defensive capabilities.

Regarding the impact of AI on employment, Winters suggested that while automation will alter job roles, it does not necessarily mean a reduction in the overall workforce. He noted that Standard Chartered has automated a significant portion of its roles, yet its headcount has increased. The bank has focused on reskilling employees, with approximately 85% of those whose roles were displaced by automation being retrained for new positions.

Winters believes that jobs requiring human judgment and interaction will remain crucial. He pointed to wealth management as an example, where despite digital tools offering investment guidance, the demand for human relationship managers persists due to continued trust in people over machines.

The CEO also discussed China's economy, observing a contrast between rapid growth in sectors like green technology and electric vehicles, and a struggling property market. He expressed confidence in China's economic outlook, citing available fiscal and monetary policy tools for growth support. Winters also commented on the resilience of Gulf economies despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, though he acknowledged significant disruptions, particularly to Qatar's gas industry.

The State Courts of Singapore. (File photo: CNA/Jeremy Long) SINGAPORE: The director of an autism spectrum disorder day activity centre was sentenced to three months and two weeks' jail on Friday (Oct 9) for cheating the social service agency that operated the centre out of S$24,750 (US$19,330).
Steven Tan Teck Liang, 63, was the director of Blue Cross Thong Kheng Autism Spectrum Disorder Day Activity Centre at the time of the offence. He had been in the position since 2017.

Tan pleaded guilty to an amalgamated charge of cheating at the State Courts. The names of others involved in this case have been redacted from court documents. The social service agency he cheated was Thong Kheng Welfare Services Society, which operates centres serving people with special needs, including the one Tan was director of.

In April 2024, Blue Cross hired six new foreign workers, and Tan arranged for them to be housed at his mother's flat. He did not tell Thong Kheng Welfare Services Society that the flat belonged to his mother.
Tan asked his brother to draw up a tenancy agreement dated Apr 1, 2024, and arranged for it to be sent to the chief executive of Thong Kheng Welfare Services Society.

SINGAPORE – Singapore has reached out to the Thai authorities for more details after Thailand announced that it would cut egg exports by up to 50% until December due to losses sustained during recent heavy floods.

In response to a media query, the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) said on Oct 7 that it is monitoring the developments and has engaged local importers. Singapore’s supply of eggs is well-diversified, it said, adding that the country is able to obtain its eggs from other sources if needed.
The Republic imports eggs from more than 10 countries, including Malaysia, Indonesia and Ukraine, with less than 15% of Singapore’s egg supply coming from Thailand, said SFA.

It added that local egg production also provides an additional source of supply during disruptions. A Thai commerce ministry official had said on Oct 6 that companies were asked to cut egg exports by 30% to 50% until December after heavy flooding killed a significant number of hens.

Jirawuth Suwanna-arj, deputy director-general of Thailand’s Department of Internal Trade, said some three million hens at egg farms in flood-hit areas of Chachoengsao province, about two hours east of the capital Bangkok, were killed.

SINGAPORE – Nine people were taken to hospital on Oct 7 after a multi-vehicle accident on the TPE left a motorcycle in flames just before the morning peak-hour rush.
The police and the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) were alerted to the accident between a car, a lorry and two motorcycles on the TPE towards PIE, after the Punggol Road exit, at about 6.50am.
A 40-year-old male lorry driver, six lorry passengers, aged between 21 and 61, and two male motorcyclists, aged 25 and 37, were taken conscious to hospital, said the police.

body: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has congratulated Saleumxay Kommasith on his recent appointment as the Prime Minister of Laos. Wong extended an invitation for Kommasith to visit Singapore, underscoring the strong and warm relations between the two nations.

Bilateral cooperation between Singapore and Laos has seen significant growth in recent years, particularly in sectors such as energy, carbon credits, and the fight against transnational crime. The relationship has been described as "very good and warm" by PM Wong.

Saleumxay Kommasith, formerly a deputy prime minister, was appointed to his new role by Laos’ National Assembly on October 5, with unanimous support from the 158 members present. He succeeds Sonexay Siphandone, who has moved to become president of the National Assembly.

PM Wong pointed to the Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project as a prime example of successful collaboration. This initiative, which commenced in 2022, facilitates Singapore's import of hydropower from Laos via Thailand and Malaysia, advancing regional electricity connectivity.

Singapore also reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Laos' development through training programs offered via the Singapore Cooperation Programme and the Initiative for Asean Integration. This year marks 25 years of development cooperation between the two countries, a partnership Singapore intends to continue strengthening in line with Laos' development goals.
Extending the invitation for an official visit, PM Wong expressed his eagerness to collaborate closely with Prime Minister Saleumxay to further advance bilateral relations.

A view of the Supreme Court in Singapore. (Photo: CNA/Jeremy Long) SINGAPORE: A private-hire driver who hit a cyclist had his jail sentence replaced with a fine after the High Court found that the cyclist's contributory negligence significantly reduced the driver's culpability.

Eric Yeo Seong Bee, who pleaded guilty to one charge of driving without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road, had been sentenced to one week’s jail and disqualified from driving for five years.

He appealed against the jail term, arguing that the cyclist’s own negligence should be a factor in deciding his culpability. He cited previous cases involving contributory negligence in support of his argument.

Yeo also argued that the District Judge wrongly held that he flouted traffic rules and regulations. In a judgment made available on Wednesday (Oct 7), the High Court agreed that the victim’s behaviour should have been considered and the District Judge erred in failing to do so.
It ruled that Yeo’s culpability was “significantly reduced” due to the cyclist’s negligence and replaced the jail term with the maximum fine of S$5,000 (US$3,900).

The proposed 200-hectare site could host Singapore's third liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal, power plants capable of using hydrogen-compatible natural gas, and facilities for importing electricity.

This initiative aims to bolster Singapore's energy security and support its transition towards greener energy sources. The EMA announced on October 6 that it is assessing the feasibility of this project, which is intended to meet the nation's growing electricity demand as its economy expands.

The study will evaluate the potential for approximately 6 gigawatts of domestic power generation and 2 gigawatts of electricity imports. Singapore currently relies heavily on imported natural gas, accounting for about 93% of its energy needs, with a second LNG terminal under construction and expected to be operational by the end of the decade.

To advance this feasibility study, the EMA plans to appoint a consultant by mid-2027. This consultant will be tasked with developing a masterplan for the energy cluster, considering various energy mixes, capacities, and development timelines. The study is expected to take two years to complete and will also assess technical, regulatory, environmental, and aviation considerations.

Pulau Tekong is being considered as a potential second major energy hub for Singapore, complementing Jurong Island. The island's location could also be advantageous for importing electricity from neighboring regions. The development of such a cluster could enhance energy resilience by reducing dependence on single fuel sources, technologies, or suppliers.

These schools will reserve 60 spots in Phase 2C, an increase from the current 40, for students without prior school connections. This phase prioritizes children living nearby.

A new two-track system will be introduced at these 12 schools, located in neighborhoods with less than 40% public housing. Half of the 60 reserved spots will be for children living within 2km of the school, while the other half will be for those living more than 2km away. This aims to ensure a more diverse mix of applicants.

Education Minister Desmond Lee stated that currently, fewer than 1 in 6 students entering these popular schools through Phase 2C come from public housing, a figure the MOE is monitoring. The changes are intended to widen access for children from various backgrounds and encourage greater mixing among students.

Concerns were raised by Members of Parliament about potential disadvantages for children living close to schools under the new framework. Minister Lee responded that the increased allocation for Phase 2C is specifically designed to favor those living near schools, and the two-track scheme addresses situations where proximity alone does not guarantee socio-economic diversity.

Discussions also touched upon the challenges of expanding popular schools due to infrastructure constraints and the potential impact on smaller schools. The MOE will not be using specific baseline or outcome indicators to assess socio-economic mixing, as each school and neighborhood has unique characteristics.

Agentic AI systems, capable of executing actions, interacting with external systems, and adapting their behavior with reduced human oversight, present both opportunities and risks. Mr. Tan noted that many of the risks associated with these systems are extensions of existing challenges, and current guidelines regarding human accountability, controls, and cybersecurity remain applicable.

The government is also monitoring international developments in this emerging field and is developing internal capabilities to go beyond current frameworks. This includes a focus on strengthening cybersecurity to protect systems that AI agents interact with, as well as adapting frameworks to account for the increased autonomy of these systems.

Mr. Tan welcomed frontier AI companies to take greater responsibility in managing the risks of their systems, including early identification of capabilities and risks, and implementing safeguards before widespread deployment. He stressed the importance of rectifying issues promptly if AI systems cause harm or impact others.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo added that Singapore is studying the need for new safety measures in high-risk AI applications. Potential safeguards for essential services and other high-risk uses could include more rigorous testing, verifiable evidence of safety measure effectiveness, tighter deployment controls, and stronger regulatory oversight.

The IMDA highlighted that this growth reflects the ongoing impact of digital technologies on business operations and work processes across various industries.

Tech employment also saw a rise, growing by 3.8% to 222,200 in 2025, with the fastest growth in roles related to AI, data, and cybersecurity. The median monthly salary for tech workers in 2025 was $8,000, significantly higher than the overall median for all resident workers.

Businesses using AI reported benefits such as improved productivity and processes, with nearly 88% citing these gains. Other reported advantages include cost reduction and better resource optimization. Workers also experienced benefits, with productivity improvements being the most cited advantage of AI use at work.

(File photo: iStock) SINGAPORE: Singapore's digital economy grew to S$144.1 billion (US$112.4 billion) in 2025, outpacing growth in the broader economy, while artificial intelligence (AI) adoption accelerated.

The digital economy accounted for 19.3 per cent of Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP), up from 18.8 per cent or S$136.5 billion in 2024, Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA)'s said in its Singapore Digital Economy Report released on Monday (Oct 5).

This represented a year-on-year growth of 5.6 per cent, outpacing the nominal GDP year-on-year growth of 3.1 per cent in 2025. Non-information and communications (I&C) sectors remained the dominant growth driver, making up more than two-thirds of the digital economy, said IMDA.
The nominal value-added from digitalisation in these sectors grew 3.6 per cent year-on-year to S$97 billion. Meanwhile, the I&C sector grew 6.1 per cent year-on-year to S$47.1 billion in 2025.

This expansion in both I&C and non-I&C sectors is reflected in tech employment - which grew 3.8 per cent year-on-year to 222,200 in 2025 - with roles in AI, data and cybersecurity among the fastest-growing.

body: A Singapore court has ruled that nearly S$140 million held in local bank accounts by the son of a convicted Indonesian palm oil tycoon will remain seized for an additional 12 months. This decision comes despite significant procedural lapses by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) that infringed upon the son's right to be heard.

The CPIB had failed to report the seizure of the funds by the statutory deadline, doing so approximately 10 months late. This delay meant the bureau lacked lawful authority to control the funds during that interim period. However, the judge determined that these lapses did not justify returning the money, which is suspected to be the proceeds of criminal offenses.

The funds were seized on May 17, 2023, from four bank accounts belonging to Bill Darmadi, the son of Surya Darmadi, an Indonesian palm oil magnate convicted of corruption and money laundering. Surya Darmadi was sentenced to 15 years in jail and fined a substantial amount in Indonesia for operating palm oil businesses without permits and laundering illicit profits.

CPIB investigations revealed that substantial funds had flowed from Indonesian companies linked to Surya Darmadi into Singapore-incorporated companies owned by his son, Bill Darmadi. These funds were subsequently transferred to Bill Darmadi's personal bank accounts in Singapore.

While the judge acknowledged the seriousness of the CPIB's procedural errors, including failing to notify Bill Darmadi of an extension application and provide him with the relevant report, she concluded that these issues did not necessitate the return of the seized assets. The court found a reasonable basis to believe the funds were proceeds of an offense, although a portion could not be immediately traced to Surya Darmadi's criminal conduct but will remain seized pending further High Court proceedings.
